messages.content: I want to recover camera motion and the geometry of independently moving rigid objects from monocular video. The reconstruction also needs to distinguish changes in focal length from motion in the scene.

That combines three closely related aims: estimating how the camera moves, recovering the geometry of rigid objects that can move independently, and accounting for focal-length changes rather than treating every change in the image as evidence of scene motion. Because the input is monocular video, all of these estimates have to be reasoned about from a single video stream.
What does “independently moving rigid objects” imply here?

It means the objects are treated as rigid for the purpose of recovering their geometry, while their motion need not be the same as the camera’s motion or one another’s. The aim is not merely to explain the video with one motion shared by everything in view. It is to recover geometry for objects that may move separately, alongside the camera motion.
And why call out focal length separately from camera motion?

A change in focal length can alter how the scene appears in the image, as can movement of the camera or objects. The goal specifically calls for distinguishing those explanations, rather than attributing apparent image changes to scene motion when they could reflect a focal-length change. It does not say that every possible video permits a unique distinction; that is part of why observational ambiguities also need to be characterized.
So the comparison is against a reconstruction that keeps the camera intrinsics fixed?

Yes. The specified comparison is with fixed-intrinsics multibody reconstruction, evaluated on variable-focal-length sequences. “Fixed intrinsics” identifies the comparison method’s assumption; “variable-focal-length sequences” identifies the condition under which the improvement target applies. The node does not specify a particular reconstruction algorithm or dataset.
State the error target precisely.

The target is to reduce scale-aligned reconstruction error by 20% relative to fixed-intrinsics multibody reconstruction on variable-focal-length sequences. If the comparison error under that measure were E, the target error would be 0.8E or lower. That is a target, not a claim that the reduction has already been observed.
Why does the wording say scale-aligned error rather than just reconstruction error?

Scale alignment specifies how reconstruction error is to be compared: differences attributable solely to an overall scale choice are accounted for in the error measure. That matters for monocular reconstruction, where absolute scale can be observationally ambiguous. It does not make every aspect of the recovered geometry identifiable, and it does not by itself settle how focal-length changes and motions should be separated.
Could we say the 20% goal applies to all monocular video?

No. The stated performance comparison is specifically a 20% reduction in scale-aligned reconstruction error versus fixed-intrinsics multibody reconstruction on variable-focal-length sequences. The broader recovery goal concerns monocular video, but the numerical improvement target has that particular comparison and condition.
What is meant by characterizing observational ambiguities?

It means identifying where the visual observations may not determine a unique interpretation of camera motion, object geometry, object motion, and focal-length change. Different underlying configurations can sometimes yield similar image evidence. Characterizing those ambiguities is distinct from pretending they have been resolved: it calls for describing what the video can constrain and where uncertainty or competing explanations remain.
Is the instruction to declare that focal length and motion are always separately recoverable?

No. The aim is to distinguish focal-length changes from scene motion while also characterizing observational ambiguities. Those two clauses belong together: a useful reconstruction should separate them where the observations support doing so and should not conceal uncertainty where the observations leave multiple plausible interpretations.
The other number is 90%. What exactly is it attached to?

It is the target for empirical coverage of predicted geometry confidence regions. In general terms, empirical coverage concerns how often the geometry being assessed falls within the regions predicted to contain it, across the cases used to assess coverage. The stated aim is 90% coverage; the node does not define the precise construction of those regions or the evaluation protocol.
Does 90% coverage mean that each individual geometry estimate has 90% accuracy?

No. Coverage describes the observed frequency with which predicted confidence regions contain the geometry under evaluation. It is not the same quantity as reconstruction error, and it is not a promise that every individual geometry estimate is accurate. The goal therefore has two different quantitative aspects: a 20% reduction in scale-aligned reconstruction error under the stated comparison, and 90% empirical coverage for predicted geometry confidence regions.
Could broad confidence regions meet the coverage target without making the reconstruction good?

Conceptually, coverage alone does not establish that the regions are narrow or that the point reconstruction has low error. That is why it is important not to collapse the 90% coverage target into the separate error-reduction target. The supplied goal asks for both, without specifying an additional target for confidence-region width.
Should the ambiguity discussion be kept separate from confidence regions?

They are related but not interchangeable. Characterizing observational ambiguities is about explaining which aspects of the scene and camera may be hard to infer uniquely from the video. Predicted geometry confidence regions express uncertainty about geometry, with 90% empirical coverage as their stated target. One does not replace the other: describing an ambiguity is not itself a measured coverage result, and attaining coverage would not by itself explain every ambiguity.
Let me check the scope: we are not being asked to treat every apparent enlargement as a focal-length change, are we?

Correct. The goal is to distinguish focal-length changes from scene motion, not to presume either explanation whenever an image changes. Camera motion, independently moving rigid objects, their geometry, and focal-length variation are all part of the inference problem. The wording does not prescribe a rule that assigns any particular appearance change to one cause.
Is there already a reported result for either numerical requirement?

Not in this statement. It sets objectives: reduce scale-aligned reconstruction error by 20% against the specified fixed-intrinsics multibody comparison on variable-focal-length sequences, and achieve 90% empirical coverage for predicted geometry confidence regions. Neither number is presented as a completed experimental outcome.
Then put the whole objective into one careful formulation.

Recover camera motion and the geometry of independently moving rigid objects from monocular video while distinguishing focal-length changes from scene motion. On variable-focal-length sequences, aim for 20% lower scale-aligned reconstruction error than fixed-intrinsics multibody reconstruction; also characterize observational ambiguities and aim for 90% empirical coverage of predicted geometry confidence regions.
How would you approach estimating focal-length changes alongside camera motion and the moving objects?

The proposal is to jointly optimize a spline representation of focal length, camera poses, rigid-object poses, and geometry, using background and object tracks. Rather than estimating focal length in isolation and then treating it as settled, the approach considers how all of those quantities together explain the tracked image observations. It also calls for reporting ambiguities and producing bootstrap geometry intervals.
What does “spline focal length” mean in that description?

It means representing focal length as a quantity that can vary over the video according to a spline, rather than assuming one fixed focal length throughout. The proposal does not specify the spline’s exact form, the number or placement of its parameters, or how much variation it should permit.
Why estimate it jointly with poses and geometry?

Those quantities interact in their effects on where tracked points appear in the images. If focal length is allowed to change, an apparent change in a track cannot automatically be assigned to camera motion, object motion, or geometry alone. Joint optimization gives the estimates a common set of background and object tracks to explain, while leaving the question of whether the explanation is unique to the ambiguity analysis.
When you say camera poses, do you mean the camera’s position and orientation over the video?

Yes, that is the general meaning of camera poses here: the camera configurations associated with the video observations. The rigid-object poses likewise describe the configurations of the independently moving rigid objects. The proposal names both sets of poses as optimization variables; it does not specify a particular pose representation or motion model.
And geometry is another set of variables, not something taken as known in advance?

Correct. Geometry is part of what is to be recovered through the joint optimization. The camera poses, rigid-object poses, focal-length spline, and geometry are not described as already known inputs. The specified observational inputs are background and object tracks.
What are those tracks doing in the proposal?

They provide image observations across the video: tracks associated with the background and tracks associated with objects. Taken together, they provide constraints relevant to the camera, the independently moving objects, their geometry, and focal-length variation. The proposal does not prescribe how the tracks are obtained or how any uncertain association is handled.
Would background tracks and object tracks play identical roles?

They are both evidence for the joint estimate, but their associations matter. Background tracks concern observations associated with the background, while object tracks concern observations associated with the rigid objects whose poses and geometry are being estimated. The proposal does not lay out separate formulas or weighting rules for the two kinds of tracks.
Does joint optimization mean every variable is guaranteed to be identifiable?

No. Optimizing the variables together describes how the estimates are sought; it does not guarantee that the observations distinguish every possible combination of focal length, poses, and geometry. That is why reporting ambiguities is an explicit part of the proposal rather than an afterthought.
What sort of statement counts as reporting an ambiguity?

At the conceptual level, it would identify a distinction that the available observations do not securely determine—for example, where more than one combination of estimated quantities can account for similar tracked image behavior. The proposal calls for such ambiguities to be reported, but it does not specify their exact categories or a particular reporting format.
So an ambiguity report is not the same thing as a geometry interval?

Right. An ambiguity report communicates limits on what can be distinguished from the observations, potentially involving focal length, poses, or geometry. A bootstrap geometry interval is an uncertainty summary specifically for recovered geometry. They can be related, but an interval by itself need not explain why an ambiguity arises.
What does “bootstrap” add to the geometry intervals?

In general, bootstrap intervals use variation across estimates obtained from resampled observational evidence to express uncertainty. Applied to this proposal, the intended output is intervals for geometry rather than only a single geometry estimate. The node does not specify the resampling unit, the interval construction, or a claimed coverage result.
Could I describe the bootstrap intervals as proof that the recovered shape is correct?

No. They would be reported uncertainty intervals, not proof of correctness. How informative or well-calibrated they are would have to be assessed; the proposal itself does not report an empirical result. It is especially important not to treat an interval as eliminating an observational ambiguity that the video cannot resolve.
Does the proposal prescribe a particular objective function for fitting the tracks?

No. It specifies the quantities to optimize jointly and the broad source of observations—background and object tracks—but not an objective function, weighting scheme, solver, or initialization procedure. Those details should not be read into the proposal.
Would it be fair to say that the spline is intended to prevent all confusion between zoom and motion?

That would be too strong. Allowing focal length to vary gives the reconstruction a way to represent focal-length changes while estimating camera and object motion. It does not, merely by being a spline, ensure that every focal-length change can be distinguished from motion on the available evidence. Reporting the remaining ambiguities is part of the same proposal.
If the objects are rigid, why are both their poses and their geometry optimized?

Rigidity separates two ideas: an object’s geometry describes its shape, while its pose describes how that rigid shape is situated at an observation. An independently moving object can change pose without requiring its geometry to change. The proposal jointly estimates both because the tracked images depend on how the geometry is viewed as the camera and object poses vary.
I do not want the wording to imply that the background or object tracks are perfect.

It need not. Saying that the optimization uses background and object tracks identifies its observational basis; it does not assert that the tracks are error-free. Likewise, calling for bootstrap geometry intervals recognizes that a single geometric estimate is not the whole uncertainty story. The proposal does not specify a track-quality model.
Can the proposed outputs be summarized without suggesting the work has already been done?

Yes: propose a joint estimate of spline-varying focal length, camera poses, rigid-object poses, and geometry from background and object tracks, accompanied by reports of observational ambiguities and bootstrap intervals for geometry. That describes the intended method and outputs, not completed estimates or demonstrated performance.
Is there anything in that summary that fixes how many moving objects there are?

No. “Rigid-object poses” and “object tracks” allow for independently moving rigid objects, but the proposal does not specify an object count. It also does not prescribe the video length or the number of tracks.
Then the essential distinction is between what is estimated, what is observed, and what uncertainty is reported?

Exactly. The jointly estimated quantities are spline focal length, camera and rigid-object poses, and geometry. The stated evidence is background and object tracks. The proposed uncertainty-related outputs are reports of ambiguities and bootstrap geometry intervals. Keeping those roles distinct makes the proposal clear without claiming that the estimates are uniquely determined or that the intervals have already achieved a particular empirical coverage.
When do background parallax and object tracks actually distinguish focal-length drift from forward camera motion and object translation?

They help when the tracked background contains enough observable depth variation that a change in viewpoint produces different motion for points at different depths. A focal-length change can make image positions expand or contract, while forward camera motion can produce a similar overall pattern. The useful distinction is that forward motion generally affects the projections of different depths differently. Object tracks add evidence about motion relative to the background, but they do not automatically make every explanation unique.
Why is forward motion so easy to confuse with focal-length drift?

In a simple perspective view, both moving the camera forward and increasing focal length can make points appear farther from the image center. If the visible points offer little variation in depth, those changes can look very similar in their image tracks. The resemblance is an observational issue, not evidence that focal length and forward translation are physically the same thing.
Can you make the depth distinction more concrete without assuming a particular video?

As a simplified illustration, take stationary background points viewed by a camera looking straight ahead, with its orientation and image center held fixed. Changing focal length scales their projected offsets from the image center by the same factor. Moving the camera forward instead changes each point’s distance from the camera; nearer and farther points generally undergo different proportional image changes. Seeing that differential behavior is what makes background depth variation informative.
Is that differential behavior what you mean by background parallax?

Yes, in this context the relevant idea is relative image motion associated with background points at different depths as the viewpoint changes. It supplies evidence beyond a single uniform expansion or contraction of the image. Whether that evidence is strong enough to separate causes depends on what the tracks visibly constrain; merely having tracks labeled as background is not a guarantee.
What if all the background tracks lie at nearly the same depth?

Then the forward-motion and focal-length explanations can become difficult to tell apart from those tracks alone. Across a narrow depth range, the depth-dependent differences produced by forward motion may be too small to distinguish clearly from a common scaling of image positions. That is a case where the ambiguity should be acknowledged rather than hidden behind one fitted explanation.
Does a background with several depths settle the question completely?

Not necessarily. Distinct depths can provide the kind of evidence needed for separation, but the observed motions also depend on camera pose and scene geometry, which themselves have to be inferred. The issue is whether the available tracks constrain those quantities well enough to make focal-length drift distinguishable from forward motion—not simply whether more than one depth exists in principle.
Where do the tracks on moving objects enter that reasoning?

They show how each observed rigid object behaves in the image alongside the background. If a pattern appears in both the background and an object’s tracks, that can inform an explanation involving the camera or focal length; if an object’s tracks depart from what the background supports, that can inform an explanation involving its own pose change, including translation. The comparison is useful, but object motion can still interact with camera motion and focal length in the image.
So if an object grows in the image, that alone does not prove it translated toward the camera?

Correct. Apparent growth could be consistent with object translation toward the camera, a focal-length increase, camera motion, or a combination, depending on the other observations. Its tracks become more discriminating when interpreted together with background behavior and the object’s rigid geometry, rather than from apparent size change alone.
Could an object moving sideways be easier to distinguish from focal-length drift?

It can be, under favorable observations. A focal-length change has a different image-wide pattern from some sideways object translations, while an independently moving object can depart from the background’s pattern. But an object’s location, its other pose changes, camera motion, and the available tracks all affect what is observable, so sideways image displacement is not a universal test by itself.
What if the background does not show useful parallax, but the object has many tracks?

More object tracks may better constrain the object’s internally consistent rigid motion and geometry, but they do not necessarily provide an independent anchor for separating focal-length drift, camera motion, and object translation. If multiple explanations produce the same or nearly the same object-track behavior, the number of tracks alone does not remove that ambiguity.
Does rigidity at least tell us which apparent changes are object translation?

Rigidity says the object’s geometry stays fixed as its pose changes. That links its tracks through a common shape, which is useful. It does not say that every change in those tracks is translation: camera motion, focal-length variation, and other changes in the rigid object’s pose can also affect their image positions.
Can the background serve as the reference for deciding that an object translated independently?

It can provide a reference in the observational sense: background tracks help constrain the image changes attributable to the camera and focal length, against which object-track behavior can be compared. If an object requires a distinct motion to explain its tracks after accounting for those shared effects, that supports an independent-motion interpretation. This is conditional on the background supplying sufficient constraints; it is not a claim that the separation always succeeds.
I want to be careful about the word “distinguish.” Do we mean that the image patterns differ, or that we can uniquely recover all the underlying quantities?

Those are different claims. Differing image patterns can provide evidence for distinguishing explanations, but unique recovery of focal-length drift, forward camera motion, object translation, and geometry is stronger. The question asks when the tracks distinguish them, so the careful answer should describe conditions under which the observations are informative and also recognize cases where different underlying configurations remain observationally ambiguous.
Would a common expansion of every tracked region point to focal-length drift?

It might be consistent with focal-length drift, but it would not establish that explanation on its own. Forward camera motion can also generate outward image motion, and moving objects can contribute their own apparent expansion. The distinguishing evidence lies in details such as relative behavior across background depths and differences between object and background tracks, not merely in the presence of expansion.
And if near and far background tracks expand by different amounts?

That can be evidence of a viewpoint change such as forward camera motion, because perspective effects depend on depth. The interpretation still has to account for the camera’s other possible pose changes and the inferred geometry. It is more informative than a uniform expansion, but it should not be presented as an unconditional proof of one cause.
How should I describe a case where focal-length drift and forward motion fit almost equally well?

Describe it as weakly distinguished or observationally ambiguous on the available tracks. You can say that the background parallax does not supply enough differential evidence to separate the two reliably. If object tracks also admit more than one combination of camera, focal-length, and object motion, that limitation should be stated rather than assigning certainty to one interpretation.
Does the question imply that background parallax is required in every conceivable way of making the distinction?

No. It asks specifically when background parallax and object tracks distinguish these effects; it does not assert that they are the only possible information one could ever use. Within the question’s scope, the key is what their observed relative motions constrain and what remains ambiguous.
Can I frame the central test as whether one explanation accounts for background and object tracks together?

Yes, provided “accounts for” is not treated as proof of uniqueness. The background can constrain shared camera and focal-length effects, while object tracks can reveal behavior needing an object-specific motion. The distinction is strongest when the background shows informative depth-dependent motion and the object tracks contribute a separable pattern; it is weakest when those patterns can be reproduced by different combinations of focal-length drift, forward camera motion, and object translation.

I have a hypothesis for the distinction we were discussing: with at least 2° of background parallax and at least 1.5× depth spread, estimated focal drift has less than 5% error, despite forward motion and moving objects.

That is a specific, testable hypothesis. It proposes that when both conditions hold—background parallax of ≥2° and depth spread of ≥1.5×—focal-drift estimation has <5% error even with forward camera motion and moving objects. It should be stated as a hypothesis, not as an observed result or a guarantee for every sequence.
Do those two thresholds work separately, or is the claim about having both?
The claim is about having both. Its stated condition combines ≥2° background parallax with ≥1.5× depth spread. It does not claim that either threshold alone is enough to obtain <5% focal-drift error.
What is each condition meant to contribute to the distinction?

Conceptually, background parallax supplies evidence of viewpoint-dependent image motion, while depth spread makes differences in how background points respond to forward motion more apparent. Those differences can help separate forward motion from focal-length drift, which may otherwise produce similar-looking image changes. The hypothesis gives quantitative thresholds for those conditions, but it does not establish that they are sufficient; that is what the hypothesis proposes to examine.
Does the 2° refer to rotating the camera by 2°?

Not as written. The threshold is ≥2° of background parallax, not a specified amount of camera rotation. Equating those would change the condition. The statement also does not define exactly how background parallax is measured, so that definition would need to be made explicit before testing the hypothesis.
And 1.5× depth spread means the depths are not all nearly the same?

That captures the intended contrast in general terms: the condition calls for a spread in background depth of at least a factor of 1.5. The hypothesis does not specify which depth statistic or pair of depths defines that factor. It would be premature to substitute a particular calculation while restating the claim.
How should I read the less-than-5% part?

It is a strict error target for the estimated focal drift: <5%, not 5% or less. The wording does not define the percentage-error calculation or say whether it is assessed per sequence, across sequences, or in some other way. Those details matter for a test, but they are not results or specifications supplied by the hypothesis.
Is the hypothesis about accurately estimating the focal length itself?

It specifically concerns estimated focal drift. That points to estimating the change in focal length, rather than making a separate claim about the absolute focal length at every instant. The statement does not define a drift parameterization, so it is safest to retain the term “focal drift” rather than silently broaden the accuracy claim.
Why explicitly include forward motion?

Because forward camera motion is one of the effects that can resemble focal-length change in image tracks. The hypothesis proposes that the stated background-parallax and depth-spread conditions allow focal drift to be estimated with <5% error even when that competing motion is present. It does not say how much forward motion there is.
And the moving objects are another source of confusing image motion?

Yes. Their tracks can reflect motion independent of the camera and the background, so they complicate the interpretation of image changes. “Despite forward motion and moving objects” makes clear that the proposed focal-drift error bound is meant to hold in their presence, not only in a scene with no independently moving objects. It does not specify how many objects there are or how they move.
Does this predict that we can also estimate every object's geometry to less than 5% error?

No. The <5% prediction is for estimated focal drift. It does not assign that error bound to rigid-object geometry, object poses, or camera motion. Those quantities may be involved in explaining the observations, but the numerical claim here is narrower.
Could I say that meeting the two thresholds resolves all observational ambiguities?

That would go beyond the hypothesis. It proposes a particular level of focal-drift estimation accuracy under two stated observational conditions, despite forward motion and moving objects. It does not claim unique recovery of every pose and geometry variable, or that no ambiguities remain.
What if a sequence has enough parallax but less than 1.5× depth spread?

Then it does not satisfy the hypothesis’s combined condition. The hypothesis makes no prediction that focal-drift error must be below 5% in that case, but it also does not claim that accurate estimation is impossible. Failing a stated condition is not the same as proving the opposite outcome.
The same would apply if depth spread is adequate but parallax is below 2°?

Exactly. With less than 2° of background parallax, the stated condition is not met, even if depth spread reaches ≥1.5×. The hypothesis does not specify what the focal-drift error would be for that case.
Are the threshold values inclusive?

Yes. The ≥ symbols include exactly 2° of background parallax and exactly 1.5× depth spread. By contrast, the predicted error is strictly below 5%; an error of exactly 5% would not satisfy that part of the hypothesis.
Should I present the thresholds as established physical cutoffs?

No. They are thresholds in the proposed hypothesis. The statement does not establish that 2° and 1.5× are universal boundaries between distinguishable and indistinguishable cases. Their proposed relationship to <5% focal-drift error would need to be assessed rather than assumed.
If an estimate comes out under 5% error, does that prove the two conditions were necessary?

No. The hypothesis says that focal-drift error is <5% when both stated conditions hold in the presence of forward motion and moving objects. It does not say that <5% error can occur only under those conditions. Accuracy outside the thresholds would not, by itself, contradict the claim as stated.
What distinction is this hypothesis trying to make operationally?

It links observable background structure and motion to the accuracy of separating focal drift from competing motion. The idea is that ≥2° background parallax together with ≥1.5× depth spread may provide enough differential evidence for a focal-drift estimate with <5% error, even when forward camera motion and moving objects complicate the image tracks. That proposed link—not a completed demonstration—is the substance of the hypothesis.
Can you give me a concise version that keeps every qualification?

Hypothesis: With ≥2° background parallax and ≥1.5× depth spread, estimated focal drift has <5% error despite forward camera motion and moving objects. Both observational thresholds are required by the stated condition; the claim concerns focal-drift error, not error for all reconstructed quantities, and it remains a hypothesis rather than a reported finding.
How would we investigate when the tracks actually distinguish zoom from motion?

The plan is to sweep background parallax, depth spread, zoom, and forward and object motion in ZoomRigid, then measure focal error, reconstruction error, and interval coverage. Varying those conditions is intended to show how the measured outcomes change across different observational situations. This is a planned evaluation, not a report of results.
What does “sweep” mean here?

It means examine a range of conditions rather than only one configuration. Background parallax and depth spread describe aspects of the available background evidence; zoom and forward and object motion concern the changes that the reconstruction must disentangle. The plan does not specify ranges, increments, or a particular arrangement of combinations.
Why include both background parallax and depth spread?

They are related but distinct. Parallax concerns the observable image displacement associated with viewpoint change, while depth spread concerns variation in the depths of background points. Sweeping both can examine whether the available background tracks provide enough depth-dependent evidence to distinguish focal changes from forward motion. The plan does not presume in advance which combinations will suffice.
Wouldn't zoom and forward motion both make things appear to grow?

They can produce similar-looking changes, which is why both are included. Varying zoom alongside forward motion lets the evaluation examine focal error and reconstruction error under differing degrees of potentially confusable image change. The plan does not assert that every combination can be distinguished.
And what is the purpose of varying object motion too?

Independently moving objects add image changes that need not come from zoom or camera motion. Including object motion lets the evaluation address that complication rather than examining only a background and moving camera. The plan does not fix particular object trajectories or motion amounts.
Does “forward/object motion” mean they have to change together?

Not necessarily. The wording names forward motion and object motion among the conditions to sweep, but it does not say whether they are varied independently, jointly, or in a particular sequence. It would be unwarranted to read a specific sweep design into that shorthand.
Why specify ZoomRigid by name?

ZoomRigid is the named setting for this planned sweep. Saying the sweep occurs in ZoomRigid preserves where the evaluation is intended to take place. The plan does not, by itself, describe ZoomRigid's construction or establish any result from it.
What does each of the three measurements tell us?

Focal error addresses the accuracy of the estimated focal behavior. Reconstruction error addresses the recovered scene quantities more broadly, without being interchangeable with focal error. Interval coverage assesses how often the reported intervals contain the geometry they are meant to cover. Looking at all three avoids treating a good focal estimate as proof of good reconstruction or well-calibrated intervals.
Are those three outcomes all to be measured throughout the sweep?

That is the plan as stated: sweep the named conditions in ZoomRigid and measure focal error, reconstruction error, and interval coverage. It does not spell out the exact measurement schedule or aggregation, so I would not claim a particular number of runs or observations per condition.
Could low focal error still come with high reconstruction error?

Conceptually, yes. The measurements concern different aspects of the estimation problem. Including both in the plan allows the evaluation to reveal whether accurate focal estimation accompanies accurate reconstruction under the conditions examined, rather than assuming that one guarantees the other.
And could reconstruction error look good while the intervals have poor coverage?

Yes, those are also distinct assessments. A reconstruction-error measure evaluates estimation error, whereas interval coverage evaluates whether the reported uncertainty regions contain the geometry with the observed frequency. Measuring both makes it possible to assess accuracy and uncertainty reporting separately; the plan does not state how either will turn out.
What does changing background parallax help us learn if zoom is also changing?

It lets the evaluation examine how the amount of background viewpoint evidence relates to focal error when zoom is present. The question is whether more or less informative background motion changes how well focal variation can be distinguished from scene motion. Without measured outcomes, we cannot say where that distinction will become reliable.
Why not just sweep zoom and hold everything else fixed?

That would not cover the question the plan addresses. The difficulty of distinguishing focal variation from motion can depend on background parallax, background depth spread, forward camera motion, and independently moving objects. The stated plan explicitly sweeps all of those factors alongside zoom so their relationship to the measured outcomes can be examined.
Does this commit us to a particular zoom pattern?
No. It commits to sweeping zoom in ZoomRigid, but supplies no zoom range, temporal pattern, or parameterization. Those specifics cannot be inferred from the plan.
Does it say how depth spread will be calculated?

No. Depth spread is a named sweep dimension, but its calculation and the values to include are not specified here. The same caution applies to how parallax, motion amounts, and errors will be operationalized.
I don't want the wording to suggest that we have already found the identifiable region.

Then keep it prospective: the sweep is intended to examine when background and object tracks supply useful distinctions among zoom, forward motion, and object motion. Measuring focal error, reconstruction error, and interval coverage across the swept conditions may reveal patterns, but the plan itself does not identify a region or report a threshold.
Would a high interval-coverage measurement settle the ambiguity question?

Not by itself. Coverage is about how often intervals contain the geometry they are intended to cover. Ambiguity concerns whether the observations distinguish different underlying explanations. The coverage measurement is relevant to uncertainty reporting, but it cannot simply be substituted for an analysis of focal error and reconstruction behavior across the swept conditions.
If the background is informative, can object motion still complicate the interpretation?

It can. Background evidence may help constrain effects shared across the image, while object tracks reflect independently moving rigid objects as well. Sweeping object motion along with the background conditions allows the planned measurements to address that complication. It does not assume that background evidence always removes it.
What should we avoid saying about the planned measurements?

Avoid saying that focal error is already low, reconstruction error has already improved, or interval coverage has already reached a particular level. Also avoid specifying an unprovided sweep grid or claiming that any one factor has been shown to cause a particular outcome. At this point, the content is the planned variation of conditions in ZoomRigid and the three quantities to measure.
Give me a short formulation of the plan that doesn't imply an outcome.

In ZoomRigid, sweep background parallax, depth spread, zoom, forward motion, and object motion; measure focal error, reconstruction error, and interval coverage across the examined conditions. The measurements are intended to inform when the available tracks distinguish focal changes from motion, without presupposing the answer.
For the next activity, render 480 ZoomRigid sequences that straddle 2° background parallax and 1.5× depth spread, with forward camera motion and object motion, and measure focal-drift error.

That sets out a focused activity: render 480 sequences in ZoomRigid, include conditions on both sides of the 2° parallax and 1.5× depth-spread thresholds, include forward and object motion, and measure the error in estimated focal drift. It specifies what to generate and measure, but does not report an error result.
What does “straddle” commit us to here?

It means the rendered sequences should cover conditions below and above the named thresholds, rather than all lying on one side. The activity does not specify how many of the 480 sequences fall on each side, whether any fall exactly at a threshold, or the precise values used.
Do we need to straddle both thresholds?
Yes. The wording names 2° parallax and 1.5× depth spread, so the activity concerns variation around each of them. It does not specify a particular grid of parallax–depth-spread combinations.
Is the 2° value a camera-rotation setting?

Broadly, a gauge concerns representational freedom: more than one assignment of reconstruction quantities can be consistent with the same image evidence. No. Identifying an ambiguity tells us that the observations may not securely select one explanation.
